items.title: Chalmers rejects the Spender CGT plan as housing tax bills stall in the Senate (ABC, 17 November 2026)
items.summary: The Treasurer rejected an independent MP's alternative capital gains tax plan as housing tax bills stall in the Senate, with the 50% CGT discount due to end for gains from July 2027. items.title: Vinnies poll pushes Victorian parties to fund homelessness prevention (CathNews, 17 November 2026)
items.summary: A charity-commissioned poll of 648 Victorians found 49% ranked preventing homelessness first, and the charity is using it to press parties to fund prevention. Use it for how NGOs shape homelessness policy, noting the poll was opt-in and not representative.

items.title: Underquoting laws fail to make Victorian price guides reliable — and NSW pauses its reforms (November 2026)
items.summary: The card now records that NSW paused its underquoting reforms until 1 December 2027, hours before they were due to start on 17 November 2026. It now compares the rules as legislated with the paused position, a useful case on whether protection for buyers works without enforcement.

items.title: Dut v R [2026] NSWCCA 184 — backdating for quasi-custody is a matter of discretion
items.summary: A man sentenced for supplying a large commercial quantity of methylamphetamine appealed only on how far his start date was backdated for refused bail, strict bail conditions and a residential detox, and the Court of Criminal Appeal dismissed the appeal. It shows that quasi-custody is a matter of fact whose weight is discretionary, in a short judgment on a single point.

items.title: R v Haouchar [2026] NSWDC 417 — re-sentencing after a successful appeal: an aggregate sentence and Form 1 offences
items.summary: After a successful appeal against convictions on other offences, a man was re-sentenced to an aggregate of 6 years for a police pursuit, an unauthorised pistol, commercial drug supply with two Form 1 offences and dealing with proceeds of crime. It is a clear example of re-sentencing after appeal, aggregate sentencing and how Form 1 offences are taken into account.

items.title: R v Rokomaqisa (No 11) [2026] NSWSC 665 — client legal privilege protects the DPP's conference notes
items.summary: In a murder-conspiracy retrial, the Supreme Court held that the DPP's conference notes and emails about a witness were protected by client legal privilege, that limited disclosures did not waive it, and that the rest of the material could not bear on a fact in issue. It shows the limits of defence subpoenas for prosecution files, in an interlocutory ruling.

items.title: R v Rokomaqisa (No 13) [2026] NSWSC 813 — a recorded conversation is relevant and s 66A answers hearsay
items.summary: In the same retrial, the defence sought to exclude a recorded 2021 conversation between three other men as irrelevant hearsay, but the Court held it relevant to the conspiracy count and that s 66A removes the hearsay objection. It is an example of the hearsay rules and the exception for statements about a person's intention, in an interlocutory ruling.

items.title: R v Rokomaqisa (No 16) [2026] NSWSC 960 — prejudice from a police witness is curable, so the jury stays
items.summary: When a police witness mentioned the accused's associates and 'police holdings', the defence applied to discharge the jury, but the Court held that any prejudice was minor and curable by directions. It shows the test for discharging a jury, which is whether it is necessary to prevent a miscarriage of justice, in an interlocutory ruling.

items.title: R v Rokomaqisa (No 19) [2026] NSWSC 1391 — a detective's opinion on organised crime networks admitted
items.summary: On a voir dire, a Detective Inspector's opinion on how organised criminal networks operate was admitted as relevant and based on specialised knowledge from police experience, and breaching the Expert Witness Code did not bar it. It shows how courts decide whether opinion evidence is admissible, in an interlocutory ruling.

items.title: R v Rokomaqisa (No 22) [2026] NSWSC 1394 — late disclosure by the Crown sinks expert phone evidence
items.summary: The Crown's expert wanted to say that a phone at the accused's home was a second encrypted device, but the Court excluded the evidence because it relied on a partial extraction served only on the day, with the fault mainly the Crown's. It shows how late disclosure can sink prosecution evidence and the duty of disclosure in an adversary system.

items.title: R v Rokomaqisa (No 25) [2026] NSWSC 1397 — a CCTV still with a wrong timestamp excluded as misleading
items.summary: The defence tried to tender a police still from council CCTV whose timestamp was 12 seconds different from the original footage, and the Court excluded it as misleading and confusing because the gap came from making the still. It shows the discretion to exclude evidence and the importance of the integrity of electronic evidence.

items.title: Should Australia adopt a staggered age of consent? (The Conversation, 16 November 2026)
items.summary: An academic opinion piece asks whether Australia should cap the age gap for 16- and 17-year-olds who can legally consent, setting a UK proposal against Australia's single age of consent, special care offences and similar-age defence. items.title: The Coalition's 'Luke's Law' would make bail refusal automatic (Moree Online News, 16 November 2026)
items.summary: The Coalition's 'Luke's Law' would replace case-by-case bail assessment with automatic refusal for anyone charged with a serious offence while on bail, as remand already makes up a record 46% of adults in custody. It tests the presumption of innocence against community protection and law reform driven by election promises, although NSW publishes no data on offences committed on bail.

items.title: Chimmalee v R [2026] NSWCCA 188 — no miscarriage in a fraud plea, and the sentence stands

It shows how hard it is to withdraw a guilty plea on appeal and the limits of appeals against sentence.

items.title: Gamage v DPP (NSW) [2026] NSWCA 243 — no jurisdictional error in District Court interlocutory rulings
items.summary: A man convicted of three ICAC Act offences sought judicial review of two District Court orders before his appeal was heard, and the Court of Appeal found no jurisdictional error. items.title: Kinnaird v R [2026] NSWCCA 192 — general deterrence and parity for child abuse material offences

items.title: State of NSW v Shields (Preliminary) [2026] NSWSC 1427 — an interim supervision order for a high-risk sex offender, with monitoring removed
items.summary: At a preliminary hearing on the State's application for a new two-year extended supervision order, the Supreme Court appointed experts and made a 28-day interim order, removing electronic monitoring given the offender's progress. It shows post-sentence supervision balancing community protection against liberty; the final order is undecided.

items.title: Victorian Coalition pledges a Dhurringile bootcamp for young offenders (ABC, 15 November 2026)
items.summary: The Victorian Coalition has pledged a bootcamp for 14–17-year-olds at the former Dhurringile Prison, reviving a model Queensland abandoned in 2015 after 63.5% of sentenced participants reoffended. It tests detention as a last resort and election politics driving youth justice law, though no cost, capacity or opening date has been released.

items.title: WE v R [2026] NSWCCA 189 — a terrorism conviction quashed because fitness to be tried was never tested
items.summary: A terrorism conviction from a fourth trial was quashed because the accused, who represented himself, was later diagnosed with schizophrenia present during the trial, and the Crown conceded that fitness to be tried had never been tested. It shows fitness to stand trial as a safeguard of a fair trial, with a retrial required to test fitness first.
items.note: Content note: this item involves terrorism. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Town Hall protest prosecutions — defence subpoena for police documents upheld (Local Court of NSW, 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds a second summary of the 11 November report on the subpoenas, naming the three ministers as the Premier, the Police Minister and the Tourism Minister and noting that 27 people were arrested on the night. It also notes that reported counts of those charged vary over time, and every accused is presumed innocent.

items.title: Activists keep copyright but must destroy covert abattoir footage (ABC, 11 November 2026)
items.summary: The High Court refused to give an abattoir the copyright in activists' covert footage, which protects media and third parties, but still ordered the activists, who had trespassed seven times, to destroy their copies. It shows the courts balancing property and copyright against the public interest in publication, with damages of $130,000 ordered below.

items.title: Moltter v Aboriginal Housing Office [2026] NSWCATAD 351 — an age discrimination complaint refused leave to proceed
items.summary: A 71-year-old project manager who said she was told to retire was refused leave by NCAT to pursue her age discrimination complaint, because taking her evidence at its highest the likely reason was budget and the case was not reasonably arguable. It shows state anti-discrimination law enforced through a complaints body and a tribunal, and a leave filter that can end a complaint early.
core_labels: The role of courts and tribunals

items.title: UN toxics expert says Australia is failing on pollution and climate (AAP, 8 September 2023)
items.summary: A UN toxics expert who visited Australia for 12 days in 2023 criticised its fossil fuel plans and pollution standards, and Australia has since accepted only 128 of 332 UPR recommendations. It is a clear case of UN scrutiny resting on state consent, alongside the General Assembly's 161–0 vote recognising a right to a healthy environment.
core_labels: The role of the United Nations

items.title: NT and Queensland shut a UN expert out of youth detention — and his end-of-mission findings (November 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds the Special Rapporteur's end-of-mission findings of 13 November, in which he called the state of Indigenous rights 'embarrassing' and made preliminary recommendations, with the final report due at the Human Rights Council in September 2027. A table sets those recommendations against the government's position, and notes that they are not binding and Commonwealth law cannot compel a state to admit a UN visitor.
core_labels: The role of the United Nations

items.title: Ashdown & Markin (No 3) [2026] FedCFamC1F 393 — serious violence allegations not proved; supervised time moves to unsupervised
items.summary: A mother alleged very serious violence by the father of their five-year-old daughter, but after a ten-day hearing the judge found only one allegation proved and the father not an unacceptable risk, so time moved from supervised to staged unsupervised time with sole decision-making to the mother. It shows the civil standard and cogent proof for serious claims in family violence allegations.
items.note: Content note: this item involves family or domestic violence. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Benzema & Devi [2026] FedCFamC1F 632 — a father in default; coercive control found; sole decision-making and no time
items.summary: A father who filed nothing for trial was found in default, and on the mother's unchallenged evidence the Court found coercive control, gave her sole decision-making with no time for him, and adjusted the property 67.5/32.5 for his non-disclosure. It shows non-physical family violence recognised in parenting orders and the consequences of ignoring court directions.
items.note: Content note: this item involves family or domestic violence. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Daily & Daily (No 7) [2026] FedCFamC1F 635 — spousal maintenance refused and a harmful proceedings order made
items.summary: After about eight years of litigation, a husband who had spent a $968,849 disability payout was refused spousal maintenance and barred from starting new proceedings against his former wife without leave. It shows the limits of spousal maintenance and the harmful proceedings order as a way of controlling repeated litigation.

items.title: Hult & Ezra [2026] FedCFamC1F 627 — a solicitor's 'cavalier' withdrawal on the first day of trial referred to the regulator
items.summary: On the first day of a final hearing listed for ten months, a wife's lawyers sought to withdraw over unpaid fees, and the judge referred the solicitor to the Legal Services Commissioner without finding any breach. It shows the court's control of its own process and how late withdrawals affect access to justice.

items.title: Merckx & Merckx [2026] FedCFamC1F 693 — an arbitration award that could not be registered
items.summary: A couple arbitrated their property dispute, but with no written agreement meeting reg 67F and no reg 67G notice it was not family law arbitration, so the award could not be registered. It shows the formal requirements that make arbitration an enforceable alternative to court.

items.title: Nurse carries a colleague's baby as the ALRC surrogacy review nears its end (ABC, 15 November 2026)
items.summary: A Queensland nurse carried a colleague's baby through lawful altruistic surrogacy as the ALRC nears the end of its review, while only 103 babies were born through domestic surrogacy at ANZ clinics in 2024 and most Australians go overseas. It illustrates how law and technology interact in birth technologies and the case for reform, with commercial surrogacy carrying up to three years' jail in Queensland.

items.title: Police prosecutor convicted of 11 DV offences faces sentence (ABC, 12 November 2026)
items.summary: A police prosecutor found guilty by a jury of 11 domestic violence offences against his wife faces sentence, and the LECC found that only 15 of 56 officers investigated for domestic violence were charged. It shows accountability when an officer is the offender and the criminal process from verdict to sentence; the card keeps to the legal process.

items.title: Weaponising the Family Court — systems abuse after separation (SMH, 14 November 2026)
items.summary: A Sydney Morning Herald feature argues that the legal process itself can become a tool of abuse after separation, with 83% of 2023–24 final parenting applications alleging family violence. It shows that reforms such as harmful proceedings orders and subpoena limits depend on money and on judges choosing to use them, though the cases are told from the parents' side.

items.title: Ysmaiylova & Sedlakova [2026] FedCFamC1F 664 — leave for a stepfather to start adoption proceedings
items.summary: A stepfather and mother sought leave to start adoption proceedings for her 13-year-old son with the biological father's consent, and the Court granted leave, giving the child's wishes substantial weight. It shows that leave is more than procedural and how the court balances parental consent and a child's views.

items.title: State planning power shuts a council's free homeless camp in Moreton Bay (AAP, 13 November 2026)
items.summary: A Queensland council opened a free legal camp for homeless people after a court found earlier evictions breached the Human Rights Act, but a state planning law shut it about three months into a 12-month trial. It shows state law overriding a local response to homelessness in a state with no right to housing.

items.title: 6,437 supportive homes could end rough sleeping in NSW (Per Capita for Homelessness NSW, October 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds a second summary noting that rough sleeping in NSW has risen 75% since 2020, and frames the Housing First plan against the right to adequate housing. The 6,437-home estimate remains advocacy research commissioned by those who would deliver the homes.

items.title: Hunter social housing queue nears 6,400 as the NSW list hits a record (Newcastle Herald, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds a second summary of the same report giving the median wait for general applicants who were housed as 15.6 months in September 2026. It adds a measure of how long households actually wait to the record 72,232-household list.

items.title: Northern Rivers flood pod villages wind down as the 2027 end nears (NSW Government, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds a second summary of the release noting that residents hold occupancy agreements, not clear tenancies, and that the advocacy group House You counted 157 or more households still in the villages in September 2026. That count is not government data, so it is a useful check on the release's account.

items.title: Funding Solved Pty Ltd v Aravanopoulos [2026] NSWSC 1440 — a guarantor's unconscionability defences fail
items.summary: A woman who guaranteed her company's loan and mortgaged two properties argued unconscionable conduct and an unjust contract, but the Supreme Court rejected every defence because she was experienced and advised and it was a business loan. It is a Year 11 example of contract law, unconscionability and the burden of proving a defence.

items.title: McLean v Quirk-Orford [2026] NSWCATCD 138 — an oral cost-plus renovation, defects and $29,281.70
items.summary: An owner who ran a renovation alongside an uninsured builder under an oral cost-plus deal had most claims rejected by NCAT but was awarded $29,281.70 for defects such as wet-area tiling. It is a Year 11 example of an oral contract, proof of defects and a tribunal resolving a consumer dispute.

items.title: Singh v Tian Hock Development Pty Ltd [2026] NSWSC 1432 — overstating a payment claim is not fraud on an adjudicator
items.summary: Home owners who served no payment schedule faced a builder's $201,200 adjudication, and the Supreme Court held that overstating a payment claim is not fraud on an adjudicator because the Act lets owners respond. It is a Year 11 example of the security of payment scheme, with the owners' failure to respond fatal and fraud not proved.

items.title: Coroner cannot rule out homicide after a flawed Wilcannia police investigation (ABC, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: A coroner could not decide between suicide and homicide in an Aboriginal woman's death in Wilcannia because a junior detective's first investigation lost evidence that a later homicide team could not recover, and made five recommendations. It shows how evidence lost in the first days cannot be repaired and the Coroners Court testing police work, though recommendations are not binding and the card rests on a regional report with no NSW Police response.
items.note: Content note: this item involves a death or killing. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Crown appeal lifts the sentence for child abuse committed at 15, but the survivor says it still falls short (ABC, 11 November 2026)
items.summary: On a Crown appeal, an adult sentenced for sexual abuse he committed as a 15-year-old in the 1990s had his head sentence raised from 2 years 7 months to 4 years 7 months, though the survivor says it still falls short. It illustrates Crown appeals against sentence and the victim's voice in sentencing and its limits, but the appeal reasons were not yet published, so the legal basis of the appeal cannot be confirmed.
items.note: Content note: this item involves sexual offences. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Estate of Croft v MTH [2026] HCA 44 — a survivor can use her abuser's convictions in a civil claim; new trial ordered
items.summary: All five High Court justices held that criminal convictions are admissible in a civil claim against the offender's estate, but ordered a new trial because the Court of Appeal's $1.346m award rested on a wrong assumption about the certificate of conviction. It shows how a conviction becomes evidence in a civil case, the criminal and civil standards of proof, and a survivor's civil route to compensation, with credibility findings still to be redone.

items.title: R v CL [2026] NSWSC 101 — a 16-year-old convicted of murder as a non-stabber receives 14 years 6 months
items.summary: A 16-year-old convicted of murder and armed robbery causing wounding was sentenced as a non-stabber, because the Crown could not prove who stabbed the victim, and received 14 years 6 months, with youth, deprivation and impairment reducing his culpability and the 20-year standard non-parole period not applying. It is an example of sentencing children for the most serious crime and of joint criminal liability, and he is identified by initials only.
items.note: Content note: this item involves a death or killing. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Staunton v Zahab (No 3) [2026] FCA 1639 — a control order confirmed after a terrorism sentence, but without electronic monitoring
items.summary: A man released after nine years for supporting Islamic State had his control order confirmed on a real and unacceptable risk, but electronic monitoring was removed as disproportionate, and his claimed change was untested because he did not give evidence. It shows post-sentence control weighing liberty against community safety, with each condition tailored and supportive conditions serving rehabilitation and protection together.
items.note: Content note: this item involves terrorism. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Tran v R [2026] NSWCCA 187 — bail pending a retrial after a drug importation conviction is quashed
items.summary: After his drug importation conviction was quashed, a man seeking bail before a retrial showed cause through the ceiling principle and time already served, and fourteen conditions made the risks acceptable. It is a clear example of bail after a successful appeal, balancing liberty against flight and reoffending, though it is a short bail judgment and the retrial outcome is unknown.

items.title: Town Hall protest prosecutions — defence subpoena for police documents upheld (Local Court of NSW, 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds an ABC report that seven people, including the Premier, the Police Minister and senior police, have been subpoenaed over the 9 February rally, after police withdrew 10 of about 30 prosecutions when the Court of Appeal held the PARD scheme invalid. It also gives the timetable, with evidence due on 8 March 2027 and a joint trial from July 2027, and tests rights to protest in NSW without a human rights act; every accused is presumed innocent.

items.title: Dozens of inquests reveal mental health care failures in NSW prisons — and a psychiatrist says Corrections should not run it (ABC, 31 October and 8 November 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds an ABC report of 10 November that the NSW branch of the psychiatrists' college backs a health-led overhaul, saying isolating suicidal prisoners in monitored safe cells is a security response, not health care. It also cites an estimated $550–600m a year shortfall in NSW Health frontline mental health staffing and the relevant standards, and notes that no reform has yet been adopted.
items.note: Content note: this item involves a death or killing. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Black v R; Trautsch v R [2026] NSWCCA 185 — former police officers' sentences cut for errors with aggravating factors
items.summary: The card now adds a second class summary of the ABC report, which notes that Black's original non-parole period was 3 years 3 months, with parole eligibility in November 2028. It is a small addition to the earlier media coverage, and the Court's reasons remain the source to use for the sentencing principles.

items.title: New AI safety regulator proposed as criminal law reform is considered (The Conversation, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds an ABC report that Australia is considering a world-first criminal offence for AI developers that fail to prevent harm, with Home Affairs and the AFP working on penalties and legislation hoped for in early 2027. It explains why existing computer offences need human intent, so an AI agent crossing access controls on its own falls outside them, and compares failure-to-prevent offences for foreign bribery; the review itself has not been released.

items.title: 2208670 (Refugee) [2026] ARTA 2691 — a Mexican woman abused by a church's inner circle is a refugee
items.summary: A Mexican woman, who gave new evidence at her 2026 hearing, was found credible and a refugee because state protection, changing her behaviour and relocation all failed, and the refusal was set aside after six years. It shows protection where a state cannot or will not protect and merits review correcting a refusal, though the delay is itself a measure of effectiveness; the applicant is identified by number only.

items.summary: A Chinese man added claims to be gay and celibate four years into his application, and the Tribunal was not satisfied of the claim, found family disapproval was not serious harm and affirmed the refusal. It shows credibility and timing deciding a refugee claim, in contrast with the earlier Malaysian case where a similar claim was accepted; he should not be presented as a gay refugee, and the applicant is identified by number only.

items.title: Bechelli v CBA; Giordano v CBA [2026] NSWCATAD 347 — leave refused on disability claims, granted on a sexual harassment complaint
items.summary: After a bank manager locked a woman's account, NCAT refused leave on her disability discrimination complaint and her carer-cousin's associate claim, but let the cousin's sexual harassment complaint proceed to a case conference. It shows state anti-discrimination law enforced through a complaints body and a tribunal, and a leave filter that can end a complaint at the first hurdle, though the harassment allegation is untested and denied.

items.title: Bymore and Mistral (Child support) [2026] ARTA 2700 — care percentages fixed, but a late objection delays the change
items.summary: With no care calendars and conflicting evidence, the Tribunal found a father's likely care split was 62/38, but because his objection was late the new percentages apply only from July 2025. It shows merits review by a tribunal as an alternative to a court and how care after separation shapes child support, and that a missed deadline delays a real change; party names are pseudonyms.

items.title: Callan and Lancaster (Child support) [2026] ARTA 2698 — a decade-old system error is not corrected against a mother on a pension
items.summary: A system error from 2012–13 had overpaid a mother $3,563, and the Tribunal held that the Registrar's discretion to amend should not be used, giving greatest weight to the father's much better finances against her disability pension. It shows financial responsibility for children continuing after separation, with old assessments able to be reopened, and a discretion exercised by weighing each parent's circumstances; party names are pseudonyms.

items.title: Flores & Flores [2026] FedCFamC1A 196 — a 25/75 property split overturned by consent for inadequate reasons
items.summary: Both parties asked for the appeal to be allowed, and the Full Court set aside a 25/75 property split because the reasons were inadequate and the wife's health was given no weight or plainly the wrong weight. It shows that a property percentage must be explained and that health is a s 79(5) factor, with the case sent back for rehearing by a different judge; it is HSC only and a short judgment.

items.title: Victorian Labor pledges a Clare's Law disclosure scheme if re-elected (ABC, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds a second summary noting that Victoria's pledge does not yet say what would be disclosed or how, against South Australia's verbal disclosure with a specialist worker and a confidentiality undertaking. It also notes that the funding figures are election commitments, not appropriations, and that South Australian application counts vary from about 2,500 to more than 4,000 by source.

items.title: Abideen v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1708 — delay explained, but no extension without merit
items.summary: A student refused a visa partly over a document treated as a bogus degree missed two Tribunal hearings, and the Federal Court accepted his delay was explained but refused more time to appeal because the grounds had no merit. It is a Year 11 example of time limits and finality in administrative law and a court reviewing a tribunal's visa decision; it is an extension-of-time decision, not a ruling on the visa.

items.title: Ace v Boulas [2026] NSWSC 1436 — a secretly recorded phone call is excluded in a family will dispute
items.summary: In a sibling dispute over a 103-year-old mother's will, a son tried to tender a call he had secretly recorded through CCTV, but the Supreme Court held that the recording breached the Surveillance Devices Act and excluded it under s 138. It is a Year 11 example of fairness in what evidence is heard in a civil case and of objection and tender, showing s 138 is not limited to evidence obtained by police; it is a mid-hearing ruling, not the outcome of the will dispute.

items.title: Chowdhury v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] FCA 1687 — a binary visa criterion leaves no room for hardship
items.summary: A student was refused a visa because he was not enrolled in a course when the Tribunal decided, and the Federal Court held that this criterion is binary, so hardship from COVID-19, finances and depression was legally irrelevant. It is a Year 11 example of delegated legislation and the limits of a decision-maker's power, and of law applied as written even where hardship is real, with all grounds failing and $4,500 in costs.

items.title: Hatewar v Minister for Immigration and Citizenship [2026] HCA 45 — a s 501 visa refusal survives High Court review
items.summary: A man convicted of offences against family members challenged a s 501 character refusal of a return visa, and the High Court, deciding on the papers, rejected all four grounds and dismissed the application with costs. It is a Year 11 example of judicial review in the High Court and binding directions, showing that review tests legality, not whether the decision was right.

items.title: Boy, 16, charged after alleged stabbing outside Casula High School (SMH, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: A 16-year-old has been charged with wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm after an alleged stabbing outside a Sydney high school, and police refused bail; he has not been convicted. It shows how NSW treats young accused, from the presumption of innocence and bail to the Children's Court's limited jurisdiction for serious charges, and whether knife laws prevent harm.
items.note: Content note: this item involves a death or killing. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Hobart man jailed for Nazi salutes at police and in court (ABC, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: A Hobart man was jailed for two months, reportedly Tasmania's first jail term for a Nazi salute, after saluting police and again in court, with the magistrate citing personal and general deterrence. It contrasts a state magistrate's full sentencing discretion with the Commonwealth's 12-month mandatory minimum, although the card rests on a short court report with no defence or prosecution comment.

items.title: New AI safety regulator proposed as criminal law reform is considered (The Conversation, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: An overseas AI agent accessed Australian government data in June 2026 but the AFP did not investigate because no formal report of a crime was made, and the government has now proposed a frontier AI safety regulator. It shows criminal law struggling to keep up with technology, with a possible 'failure to prevent' offence raising corporate criminal responsibility, although the card rests on a short report with no outside reaction.

items.title: R v Binge [2026] NSWDC 409 — a knife attack inside a prison cell, childhood trauma and deterrence
items.summary: An inmate who joined a group knife attack in a prison cell and pleaded guilty to reckless wounding in company was sentenced to 5 years 9 months, because deterrence for prison violence outweighed the substantial reduction in his moral culpability from childhood trauma. It is a clear example of the instinctive synthesis, the standard non-parole period as a guidepost and the Bugmy principle, and of violence in custody.

items.title: R v DL [2026] NSWDC 406 — totality and an aggregate sentence after a retrial for child sexual offences
items.summary: After a retrial, a man was sentenced for five child sexual offences on top of an existing 8-year sentence, and totality shaped an aggregate sentence of 9 years with no plea discount but 2.5% for an efficient trial. It illustrates aggregate sentencing and totality, and a retrial after a jury could not agree on some counts; he is identified by initials only and the card gives no detail of the offending.
items.note: Content note: this item involves sexual offences. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Aboriginal children far less likely to be diverted from court — BOCSAR Crime and Justice Bulletin 282 (October 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds AAP's coverage of the bulletin, which includes the Aboriginal Legal Service and ministerial views but no NSW Police response, and a second summary noting that about 72% of the court gap is linked to recorded factors. It uses the Young Offenders Act's objects to frame the unexplained 8 points as a question of equality before the law.

items.title: Black v R; Trautsch v R [2026] NSWCCA 185 — former police officers' sentences cut for errors with aggravating factors
items.summary: The card now adds an ABC report of 10 November that names the two former officers, says the assault lasted about 18 minutes on body-worn video and CCTV, and gives Black's new non-parole end date of 7 September 2027. It also records the family's reaction, though the report wrongly calls the head sentence a 'maximum sentence', so it is best used alongside the Court's reasons.

items.summary: The Tribunal found a Malaysian woman credible despite inconsistencies and delay, held that lesbian women are a particular social group, and set aside the refusal of her protection visa after about four years. It shows merits review working and sexual orientation recognised in refugee law, with the Refugee Convention enforced through the Migration Act; the applicant is identified by number only.

items.title: Son who assaulted his mother gets "prison in the community" (Northern Daily Leader, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: A man in his 20s who admitted seven offences against his mother across two incidents received a one-year intensive correction order with community service and fines, not full-time jail, and the magistrate called domestic violence 'a scourge in our society'. It shows the sentencing rules for domestic violence offences in action and community-based sentences as alternatives to custody, although the court report is brief and does not report the s 4B finding.

items.title: Victorian Labor pledges a Clare's Law disclosure scheme if re-elected (ABC, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: Victorian Labor has pledged a Clare's Law scheme, letting people ask police about a partner's history of violence, and the Opposition made a similar pledge in July, so both major parties now back it. It tests whether information protects victims when Victoria's Royal Commission did not recommend one and NSW abandoned its pilot, and shows election promises borrowing another state's model, with no bill yet.

items.title: 6,437 supportive homes could end rough sleeping in NSW (Per Capita for Homelessness NSW, October 2026)
items.summary: A Per Capita report for Homelessness NSW estimates that 6,437 supportive homes by 2033 would end persistent homelessness and that yearly government savings of $227m would exceed the $187m net running cost. It shows Housing First as a response to homelessness in a state with no legal right to housing, although it is advocacy research commissioned by those who would deliver the homes.

items.title: Hunter social housing queue nears 6,400 as the NSW list hits a record (Newcastle Herald, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: A record 72,232 NSW households are waiting for social housing, almost 6,400 of them in the Hunter, while the government and the community housing sector dispute whether current investment is enough. It shows the gap between the legal framework for allocating social housing and the supply available, although the feature leans to the sector's case and was published shortly before the state election.

items.title: Northern Rivers flood pod villages wind down as the 2027 end nears (NSW Government, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: After the 2022 floods the government built 546 temporary dwellings across 11 Northern Rivers villages, and a 9 November release sets a different outcome for each of the remaining six as they wind down. It shows government as a direct provider of disaster shelter and the limits of that role, since the Audit Office found no exit plan, though the card rests on a government release with no resident or council voices.

items.title: REINSW blames NSW rental reforms as investor lending falls (Australian Conveyancer, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: The Real Estate Institute of NSW blames the 2024 tenancy reforms for falling investor lending, while the RBA points to interest rates and tax, and Sydney's vacancy rate rose to 2.5%. It shows the tension between tenants' security and investors' supply and an industry claim to test against data, but the report is one-sided and never names the reforms.

items.title: Underquoting laws fail to make Victorian price guides reliable (AFR, 10 November 2026)
items.summary: Reported industry research found that only 43% of Victorian homes sold within the first price guide buyers saw, despite detailed underquoting laws and a taskforce that issued 185 fines. It tests the effectiveness of buyer protection when rules and enforcement still fall short, as NSW adopts similar rules, although the research could not be located to check.

items.title: Younger borrowers risk being locked in "mortgage prison" (SMH, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: After five rate rises in 2026 and falling prices, recent buyers who fail a new lender's serviceability test cannot switch loans, so laws meant to stop unaffordable lending can trap existing borrowers. It shows a protective credit law with an unintended effect and hardship rights as remedies, although the card is an economic analysis and the figures measure refinancing demand, not refusals.

items.title: Peers v Eastern Health [2026] FCA 1677 — a dismissed anaesthetist's s 109 challenge to a Victorian pandemic law fails
items.summary: A dismissed anaesthetist asked the Federal Court to declare a Victorian pandemic law inoperative under s 109 of the Constitution, but the Court found no inconsistency with the Fair Work Act, no use in declarations and no standing. It is a Year 11 example of the division of powers, s 109 and a court testing a State Act against a Commonwealth Act, and is a federalism case, not a human rights case.

items.title: Aboriginal children far less likely to be diverted from court — BOCSAR Crime and Justice Bulletin 282 (October 2026)
items.summary: A BOCSAR study of 56,742 police events involving children found that, where diversion was legally available, police sent 54% of Aboriginal children's matters to court against 24% of others, leaving about 8 points of the 30-point gap unexplained by legal factors. It is evidence on police discretion under the Young Offenders Act and whether diversion is applied fairly, although the findings are associations and do not prove bias.

items.title: Black v R; Trautsch v R [2026] NSWCCA 185 — former police officers' sentences cut for errors with aggravating factors
items.summary: The Court of Criminal Appeal reduced the sentences of two former NSW police officers who pleaded guilty to common assault and unauthorised use of OC spray on a woman in distress, because gratuitous cruelty could not aggravate the assaults and their trust and authority was counted twice. It is a clear example of statutory aggravating factors and appeals against sentence, and shows that officers who abuse their position are still sentenced on correct principles.

items.title: LB v R [2026] NSWDC 405 — a speed camera photo, identification evidence and a fanciful alternative theory
items.summary: A young person's Children's Court convictions for aggravated break and enter and taking a conveyance rested on a speed camera photo of the stolen car, and the District Court held the photo admissible, not unfairly prejudicial, and the 'someone else did it' theory fanciful. It illustrates admissibility and exclusion of identification evidence and proof beyond reasonable doubt on a circumstantial case, with the young person identified by initials only.

items.title: R v RK [2026] NSWSC 1414 — a 14-year-old who prepared a terrorist act gets a community correction order, not jail
items.summary: A 14-year-old who pleaded guilty to acts in preparation for a terrorist act, an offence carrying life, received a three-year community correction order with strict device conditions instead of jail, because youth, remorse and prospects of rehabilitation outweighed general deterrence. It is a rare example of a non-custodial sentence for a very serious offence and shows the sentencing principles for children, with RK identified by initials only.
items.note: Content note: this item involves terrorism. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: SafeWork NSW v AJ Bristow & Sons Pty Limited (No 3) [2026] NSWIC 68 — guilty after sandstone blocks killed a stonemason
items.summary: A builder was found guilty of a Category 2 work health and safety offence after heavy sandstone blocks tipped and killed a subcontracted stonemason, because hiring a specialist did not remove the company's own duty and the cause of the fall did not need to be proved. It is a strict-liability regulatory offence with a company as offender, and the decision is a verdict only, with sentencing directions listed for 19 November 2026.
items.note: Content note: this item involves a death or killing. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Three charged as accessories after the alleged DV murder of Danielle Madgwick in Wagga (ABC, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: Three people were charged as accessories after the fact following an alleged domestic violence murder in Wagga and were refused police bail, with all charges unproven and no one convicted. It shows arrest, charge and bail at the earliest stage and NSW's 2024 domestic violence bail reforms, and how an accessory's liability depends on proof of the principal offence.

items.title: $250,000 reward to find and extradite alleged gang leader Anthony Pele (ABC, 6 November 2026)
items.summary: NSW is offering a $250,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and extradition of a man who is wanted on four outstanding warrants and is presumed innocent, after three years of international cooperation failed to find him. It shows how sovereignty limits domestic enforcement, since extradition depends on another country's law and goodwill, with only 19 requests sent to Vietnam since 2012 and the first arrest in December 2024.

items.title: Cash for demerit points — the black market in false driver nominations (ABC 7.30, 8 November 2026)
items.summary: An ABC 7.30 investigation found sellers on social media taking other drivers' fines and demerit points for $22 to $100 each, because the nomination system relies largely on trust and police lack the resources to detect it. It is a good example of how detection depends on inquiry or complaint, and of general deterrence in the sentencing contrast; the figures about one woman are police allegations and she is presumed innocent.

items.title: Indigenous people "very rarely" sit on SA juries, report finds (ABC, 7 November 2026)
items.summary: The South Australian Law Reform Institute made 34 recommendations on why Indigenous people very rarely sit on juries, targeting the jury roll, disqualification for criminal history and cultural safety. It tests whether a jury drawn from the roll is a jury of peers, and shows a law reform body reporting to an Attorney-General who has promised a response in due course.

items.title: Treating, not prosecuting — NSW's New Street program for children who sexually harm (SMH, 9 November 2026)
items.summary: NSW's New Street program responds to young people who have sexually harmed others through treatment rather than prosecution, and 89% of the 71 who completed it stopped, but half of referrals are turned away. It raises prevention and rehabilitation against punishment, and why the law presumes young children lack criminal capacity, although the feature is sympathetic and long-term reoffending has not been assessed.

items.title: Victorian Labor pledges $204m "rehabilitation detention" for young offenders (ABC, 8 November 2026)
items.summary: Victorian Labor has pledged $204m for court-ordered 'rehabilitation detention' of up to 12 months for young people who commit lower-level offences such as theft and minor assault. It tests the principle that detaining children is a last resort, and shows election politics driving law reform, with no costing, age range or legislation yet published.

It shows how the Constitution protects rights only indirectly and how courts balance freedom from racial vilification against free speech, but no hearing date is set and the outcome is unknown.

items.summary: The Commonwealth has directed the ACCC to develop an Australian Consumer Law safety standard controlling which e-bikes can be sold, while the states keep control of riding, with ACCC consultation open until 30 November 2026. It is a Year 11 example of law reform responding to new technology through executive methods across a federal system, although the standard has not yet been made.

items.title: Application by Matthew Milat (s 78 review) [2026] NSWSC 966 — a child offender's 43-year sentence not referred
items.summary: Sentenced in 2012 to 43 years for a murder committed when he was about 17 years 11 months old, a man applied under s 78 for an inquiry into his sentence after his appeals ended, and the Supreme Court refused because none of his complaints raised a doubt. It shows sentencing a child offender as an adult for the most serious crime, and the review mechanism that remains once appeals are exhausted.

items.title: Brooker v R [2026] NSWCCA 181 — one phrase, two readings, and no inferred error
items.summary: A drug supplier who pleaded guilty to ongoing supply and other offences argued that the sentencing judge used his other offending to inflate the seriousness of the supply, but the Court of Criminal Appeal would not infer error from words open to two readings. It illustrates objective seriousness and the use of Form 1 offences, and how appeal courts read sentencing remarks.

items.title: Gatt v R [2026] NSWCCA 182 — unchallenged expert evidence rejected without warning
items.summary: An aggregate sentence for 20 domestic violence and public justice offences was reduced on appeal from 12 to 11 years, because the sentencing judge rejected an expert's unchallenged evidence without warning, a practical injustice. It shows procedural fairness at sentencing and how an appeal court resentences, with the judges split on the final figure; it involves family violence, so keep to the legal test.

items.title: R v Xerri (a pseudonym) [2026] NSWCCA 183 — are emails 'property' for self-defence?
items.summary: A man was acquitted on appeal in the District Court after arguing that he grabbed a device to protect his emails, but on questions stated by the DPP the Court of Criminal Appeal held that, on the facts found, the emails were information, not property, and that reading them aloud was not interference. It shows the limits of self-defence of property and courts adapting old property concepts to technology; it is a narrow ruling on stated facts, guilt is not decided, and the context is domestic violence.

It shows NSW's high-risk terrorism offender scheme, which can supervise people not convicted of terrorism, balancing liberty and rehabilitation against community protection; the allegations and any final order are undecided.

items.title: Staunton v El Matari [2026] FCA 1622 — an interim control order on release after terrorism offences

It shows Commonwealth control orders operating beside state supervision orders after a sentence ends, limiting liberty for what a person might do; the card covers an interim order only, and parts of the reasons are redacted.

items.summary: A man acquitted at a jury trial was refused a costs certificate at a hearing held without an interpreter, and he argued that this made the hearing unfair. items.title: Services warn of a 'massive' support gap for teen girls in remote NT after alleged domestic violence killings (ABC News, 5 November 2026)
items.summary: NT Police figures obtained by the ABC show 233 domestic violence charges against under-18s between March and September 2026, while services warn of a 'massive' gap in support for young victims in remote communities. It shows strong domestic violence laws existing on paper without reaching remote teenagers, with NGOs and clinics as the real delivery arm; charges are not convictions, and the men charged in two alleged killings are presumed innocent.
items.note: Content note: this item involves a death or killing and family or domestic violence. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Essential workers priced out of almost all rental listings (ABC News, 5 November 2026, on Anglicare Australia's Essential Workers Report 2026)
items.summary: Anglicare Australia tested 48,776 rental listings against the full-time award wages of 16 essential occupations and found that ten of them could afford fewer than 1% of listings, with teachers faring best at 3.3%. It tests whether tenancy law and housing policy deliver affordability and not just security, although it is an advocacy report built on one March weekend of advertised listings and a single-earner benchmark.

items.title: Peak body pitches a 7.5% short-stay levy to fund NSW social housing (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.summary: A second summary of the same ABC article now tests CHIA NSW's figures, finding that almost all of the $26 billion over 10 years comes from land tax changes ($25.9 billion), while the levy itself would raise about $1.35 billion. It also adds competing estimates, with Homelessness NSW putting the levy at about $50 million a year against CHIA's $135 million, and Victoria's levy raising $85.8 million in 2025 against a $75 million forecast.

items.title: Antakirinja Matu-Yankunytjatjara Aboriginal Corporation RNTBC v State of South Australia [2026] FCA 1663
items.summary: A native title body applied under s 61 of the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth) to vary a 2011 consent determination in four limited ways, and the Federal Court allowed the narrow variation to proceed but held that a self-represented respondent could not use it to reopen who the native title holders are. It shows a determination as a living order that courts vary as the law develops; the merits of the respondent's claim were not decided, and this is a Year 11 resource with no HSC edition.

items.title: Bail laws in NSW (2026) — explainer poster with flow chart, tests and case studies
items.summary: A redesigned three-page colour class poster sets out how bail works under the Bail Act 2013 (NSW): who decides, the three tests, the 2024 domestic violence reforms and the s 22C youth test extended to 2028, with two recent cases. It works as a one-stop revision sheet for bail or remand, although some commencement dates and a section lettering were still to be checked against the consolidated Act.
items.note: Content note: this item involves family or domestic violence. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Five charged as the AFP alleges $235m fraud on federal programs — Operation Integrity Fusion (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.summary: The AFP-led Fraud Fusion Taskforce alleges $235 million in actual and potential fraud across seven investigations into the NDIS, Centrelink and other programs, with 26 search warrants executed and five people charged. It shows the Commonwealth investigation process for white-collar crime, including multi-agency detection, warrants and digital seizure at scale; all matters are allegations.

items.title: O'Connell v DPP; DPP v O'Connell [2026] HCA 41 — appeal courts must allow for the jury's advantages
items.summary: The ACT Court of Appeal overturned a jury's murder verdict as unreasonable and entered a manslaughter verdict, but a unanimous High Court held that it had not allowed fully for the jury's advantages and sent the case back. It is a clear example of the limits on appeal courts second-guessing a jury, useful for both appeals and the role of juries.
items.note: Content note: this item involves a death or killing. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: R v Sharma [2026] NSWDC 402 — act proven but not criminally responsible: the mental health impairment defence
items.summary: A man charged with wounding his wife with intent to murder was found 'act proven but not criminally responsible', because a delusional disorder stopped him reasoning about wrongfulness. The outcome is detention and Tribunal review rather than a sentence, which makes it a clear example of the mental health impairment defence; it involves family violence, so keep to the legal test.

items.title: WA serial child sex offender freed under a 41-condition supervision order (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.summary: A WA court found a man who has served 15.5 years for child sex offences to be a high risk serious offender, but made a supervision order with 41 conditions rather than a continuing detention order. It is an example of post-sentence orders weighing community protection against liberty, although the card rests on a news report because the judgment was not located.

items.title: Darwin teenager charged with terrorism and 3D-gun blueprint offences (ABC, 29 October 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds a second Top End teenager, a girl charged on 3 November with a terrorism documents offence under s 101.5, who appeared in the Youth Justice Court on 4 November with bail listed for 13 November. It notes that her best interests must be weighed at bail but the s 15AA(3AA) presumption against bail still applies, and that she cannot be named.
items.note: Content note: this item involves terrorism. The summary describes the legal decision only.

items.title: Gavin v Greenstone Financial Services Pty Ltd [2026] NSWCATAD 339 — interim reinstatement refused
items.summary: A probationary employee with endometriosis asked NCAT to reinstate her while her disability discrimination complaint is investigated, and the Tribunal applied injunction principles and refused. It shows how anti-discrimination law is enforced through Anti-Discrimination NSW and NCAT, and how hard interim relief is to win for a self-represented worker against a represented employer.

items.title: NT and Queensland shut a UN expert out of youth detention (Amnesty International, 2 November 2026)
items.summary: The card now adds ABC reporting that Cleveland held 101 children against a safe capacity of 95 in August 2025, and that First Nations young people are detained at 26 times the non-Indigenous rate. It also notes that Special Rapporteurs visit under UN terms of reference rather than OPCAT, so cooperation rests on invitation, with preliminary findings due in Sydney on 13 November 2026.

items.title: DV Commissioner warns online misogyny is outpacing the law (ABC, 5 November 2026)
items.summary: The DV Commissioner, Micaela Cronin, warns that online misogyny is shaping young men's attitudes faster than law and policy can respond, and calls for funded prevention, a digital duty of care and action on overdue recommendations. It illustrates the limits of reactive family violence law, although some study figures in the article do not match the originals.

items.title: Daphne & Nirmal [2026] FedCFamC2F 58 — family violence, unacceptable risk and graduated time
items.summary: The Federal Circuit and Family Court found that a father committed family violence and that unsupervised time with the children was an unacceptable risk, even though his intimidation conviction and AVO had been overturned on appeal. It shows how the same conduct can lead to different outcomes in the criminal and family law jurisdictions; it involves family violence and children, so keep to the legal test.

items.title: Rahman & Rahman (No 3) [2026] FedCFamC2F 1203 — no full and frank disclosure, no property order
items.summary: A husband sought 55% of the property of a 40-year marriage but repeatedly failed to disclose his overseas companies and accounts, so the court dismissed his application. It shows why full and frank disclosure is the foundation of a property settlement.

items.title: Rogge and Loos (Child support) [2026] ARTA 2605 — no calendars, so the Tribunal splits the difference
items.summary: Two self-represented parents disputed how many nights their daughter spent with each, and with no records the Tribunal set aside a 75/25 care decision and fixed care at 70/30. It shows how care percentages drive child support, and how an informal tribunal review works, and struggles, when evidence is missing.

items.title: Statham & Statham [2026] FedCFamC2F 182 — property settlement after a husband's bankruptcy
items.summary: A husband's only asset, shares giving a right to live in the family apartment, had vested in his bankruptcy trustee, yet the court divided the property and gave the shares to the wife. It is an example of the court's power to bind a bankruptcy trustee in a property settlement, and of how loan payments and housing for the children are weighed as contributions.

items.title: Peak body pitches a 7.5% short-stay levy to fund NSW social housing (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.summary: With 72,000 households on the waitlist, the Community Housing Industry Association NSW proposes a 7.5% levy on short stays, as Victoria has, to raise about $135 million a year for social housing. It shows a peak body driving law reform through a new tax, although the revenue figures come from CHIA NSW and McKell modelling and are not independently verified.

items.title: Priced out of parenthood — Sydney house prices and falling births (SMH, 5 November 2026)
items.summary: KPMG found that Sydney neighbourhoods with median house prices of $400,000 to $900,000 fell from 199 to 86 between 2019 and 2024, while Greater Sydney's 58,122 births in 2024 were a reported 20-year low. It links unaffordable shelter to whether people start families, although the analysis is unpublished and the fertility figures were not independently checked.

items.title: Tiny homes for homeless people stalled by caravan-era planning rules (ABC, 4 November 2026)
items.summary: A Southern Highlands charity's plan to put tiny homes for homeless people on private rural land has stalled because clause 77 lets a moveable dwelling be lived in long term only by the owner's household or disaster victims. It shows planning law, rather than tenancy law, deciding whether shelter is provided at all, although the account is a sympathetic local feature built on service-provider estimates.

items.title: Coalition urges a $1bn homelessness prevention push — Right Help, Right Time (4 November 2026)
items.summary: The card now includes the campaign's open letter to Premier Chris Minns, which proposes a Preventing Harm Framework to shift spending from crisis to early intervention. His defence is self-defence, which the Crown must disprove beyond reasonable doubt, and excessive self-defence could reduce murder to manslaughter; he is presumed innocent and nothing has been decided.

It illustrates discretionary public order powers and who checks them, although the account comes from the club and fans and NSW Police had not responded.

items.title: Human Rights Watch finds SA prisons isolate prisoners with disabilities (1 November 2026)
items.summary: Human Rights Watch interviewed 42 people across nine South Australian prisons and found that 12 of 14 interviewees with psychosocial disabilities had been held in solitary confinement, four of them for 15 days or longer. items.title: Mother told to pay child support to an ex she says owes her $15,000 (ABC, 2 November 2026)
items.summary: The card has been updated with comment from Dr Amira Aftab and Amy Kilpatrick, who say the scheme's trust in self-reported income, and its slow correction through tax returns, leaves victim-survivors carrying the burden of proof. It also notes that Agency Collect can garnish wages while Private Collect is unmonitored, so the true size of the debt is unknown.

items.title: A rate hike to 4.85% tests legal protections for owners and renters (ABC live blog, 3 November 2026)
items.summary: On 3 November the RBA lifted the cash rate to 4.85%, adding about $456 a month to a $600,000 loan compared with January. It lets students compare the enforceable hardship rights and AFCA complaints process open to borrowers with NSW renters, who face limits only on the timing, not the size, of rent increases.

items.title: Coalition urges a $1bn homelessness prevention push — Right Help, Right Time (4 November 2026)
items.summary: Eleven NGOs are urging a $1 billion, four-year homelessness prevention push, framing homelessness as a failure of early help. items.title: NSW firearms reforms after Bondi and the National Gun Buyback (2025–2027)

items.title: Dozens of inquests reveal mental health care failures in NSW prisons (ABC, 31 October 2026)
items.summary: An ABC review of 249 coronial inquests into NSW prison deaths found failures in mental health care in 48 of them, and Corrections did not fully support the coroners' recommendations in 10 of 32 cases. It is a ready example of accountability for people in custody, because coroners can recommend change but cannot compel it.

items.title: Post-Bondi policing bill soars as the Armed Response Command replaces Operation Shelter (SMH, 2 November 2026)
items.summary: Operation Shelter, the surge policing response to the 7 October 2023 attack, grew from $4.1 million in its first year to $41.8 million in 2025/26 and is becoming a permanent Armed Response Command of 250 rifle-armed officers. It sets community safety against the right to protest, because there are no rules on where the command may operate.

items.title: Teen refused bail after alleged wounding at a Marsden Park house party (ABC, 31 October 2026)
items.summary: A 17-year-old was refused bail after being charged with reckless wounding following a house party in Marsden Park on 30 October 2026. It is a routine example of how the Bail Act treats children: no show cause test and youth counted as a vulnerability, but the same unacceptable risk test as adults.

items.title: Younger offenders and online recruitment — headlines v the data (SMH, 1 November 2026)
items.summary: Despite warnings of a youth crime surge, young people proceeded against in court are down 8% over 15 years and stable over two, yet youth detention has risen 34% in two years. Most of that rise is remand under stricter bail laws, which makes it a useful case study of media framing against the data.

items.title: Life-sentenced childcare abuser faces 202 new NSW charges (ABC, 30 October 2026)
items.summary: A former childcare worker serving a life sentence in Queensland has now been charged with 202 further offences in NSW. He is at once a convicted prisoner and presumed innocent of the new allegations, which brings out interstate cooperation, transfer and bail for a person already in prison.

items.title: Queensland passes 'breach bail, go to jail' laws despite warnings (ABC, 30 October 2026)
items.summary: Queensland has passed 'breach bail, go to jail' laws that add a second, stricter bail hurdle and a mandatory 12 months' jail for serious offending on bail, for children as well as adults. The government admits parts are incompatible with human rights and has made override declarations, a sharp example of mandatory sentencing against judicial discretion.

items.title: SafeWork NSW v Axentra Projects Pty Ltd [2026] NSWDC 398
items.summary: A formwork company was fined $75,000, after a 25% plea discount, and ordered to publish a notice after a 16-year-old trainee fell 3.4 metres through a formwork deck. It shows how a court sets a penalty for a corporation, including the weight given to deterrence and to a guilty plea.

items.title: Secretary, Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water v Dalton [2026] NSWLEC 138
items.summary: A landholder who cleared 944.9 hectares of native vegetation was fined $90,000 and $135,000 on two counts, after a 25% discount for pleading guilty at the first opportunity. The decision shows a court using fines so that illegal clearing no longer pays, and treating a strict-liability offence as serious.

items.title: State of New South Wales v Wheatley (Variation) [2026] NSWSC 1364
items.summary: The Supreme Court held that a NSW supervision order for a high risk offender continues to bind him outside the state, subject to its terms, but refused a condition that would have forced a parole transfer to NSW. It is a post-sentencing example of balancing community safety against individual rights, though a variation ruling is not a sentence or a finding on risk.

items.title: WA Police scan 1.38 million faces in a live facial recognition trial (The Guardian, 2 November 2026)
items.summary: A five-month WA Police trial scanned 1.38 million faces and produced 122 arrests and nine false alerts, with no specific statute governing it. It sets mass biometric scanning without individual suspicion against the reasonable-suspicion test that limits other police powers, although the figures are police-supplied and the formal evaluation is still pending.

items.title: Zakaria seeks permanent stay over alleged unlawful deportation — the Crown concession and suppressed AFP evidence (2026)
items.summary: The card on the application to permanently stay two murder charges has been updated with court reporting to 3 November 2026. It still presents an abuse-of-process argument in which the court's own integrity is weighed against the public interest in a trial, drawing mainly on the defence case with the AFP's argument still to come.

items.title: Human Rights Law Centre urges a NSW Human Rights Act as a parliamentary inquiry sits (2 November 2026)
items.summary: The Human Rights Law Centre told a NSW parliamentary inquiry on 2 November that the state still lacks a human rights Act, making it the only eastern state without one. items.title: Tutoveanu v State of New South Wales [2026] FCA 1624
items.summary: The Federal Court refused leave to sue over a police report, finding the discrimination and harassment claims were not reasonably arguable and that police investigation is not a service. items.title: Sam Wood refused bail again on strangulation and assault charges (ABC, 31 October 2026)
items.summary: A man charged with strangulation and assault was refused bail twice, because strangulation in a domestic setting is a show cause offence in Queensland and the court found he posed an unacceptable risk. It shows the law protecting an alleged victim before any finding of guilt, at the cost of remand that may match any likely sentence; this is Queensland law, not NSW.

items.title: Boleno & Newcombe [2026] FedCFamC1A 191
items.summary: An appeal against orders for a child to spend supervised time with a parent until age 10 failed in the Federal Circuit and Family Court. items.title: House prices fall a seventh month as investor tax changes bite (ABC, 2 November 2026)
items.summary: Australian home values fell for a seventh month, down 1.2% in October and 6.7% below the March peak, while rents rose 5.5%, after negative gearing and capital gains tax concessions were cut. It is the first big test of tax law as a housing affordability tool, weighing gains for buyers against risks for renters and supply.

items.title: Kathy (a pseudonym) (No 2) [2026] NSWCATGD 21
items.summary: NCAT refused a late adjournment and appointed the Public Guardian for three years for an older woman with dementia, with last-resort conditions on restrictive practices. It shows a tribunal weighing a fair hearing against delay and a person's welfare.

items.title: Lee and Minister for Immigration and Citizenship (Citizenship) [2026] ARTA 2513
items.summary: The tribunal refused an extension of time to seek review of a citizenship refusal that was 347 days late, because the notice went to the email address she had nominated and she could reapply. items.title: NSW firearms reforms after Bondi and the National Gun Buyback (2025–2027)
items.summary: The card now covers the first day of the National Gun Buyback, which opened on 2 November 2026 at six stations, with initial bookings full on day one and 34 more stations from early December.
